items.title: The 14-year-old Richard II rode out to meet the rebels at Smithfield
items.claim: On 15 June 1381 the Peasants' Revolt ended at Smithfield. What actually happened?

options.text: The king's army defeated the rebels in open battle
Wat Tyler was killed by William Walworth, mayor of London, and Richard II rode forward and persuaded the crowd he would be their new leader
The rebels stormed the Tower of London and forced Richard to abdicate
John of Gaunt negotiated a settlement that gave rebels permanent rights

items.reveal_title: A teenage king and a dead leader
items.reveal:
Walworth stabbed Tyler during a parley. As Tyler fell, Richard II — aged 14 — rode forward and said 'You shall have no captain but me'. The rebels dispersed.

The charters Richard granted were revoked within weeks. John Ball was hanged, drawn and quartered in July. Richard reportedly told a later petition: 'Villeins ye are, and villeins ye shall remain.' The poll tax was nonetheless quietly dropped.
items.why: Successful revolts are rare and brief. The 1381 rising failed in its immediate aims but ended the experiment with poll taxes for 600 years — until 1990.

items.title: British abolition came in two acts, decades apart

options.text: 1807 — both the trade and slavery itself

The Slave Trade Act 1807 abolished the trade; the Slavery Abolition Act 1833 ended slavery in most British colonies from August 1834 — with £20 million paid in compensation to slave-owners, not the enslaved

items.reveal:
The 1833 Act freed around 800,000 people in the Caribbean, Mauritius and the Cape from 1 August 1834. Field workers became 'apprentices' for six years (ended in 1838 after protests). Around 46,000 claims paid out £20 million — roughly 40% of the Treasury's annual budget.

The loan to finance the compensation (UCL's 'Legacies of British Slave-ownership' project) was only paid off by the UK Treasury in 2015. Slavery in British India was not covered by the 1833 Act; the Indian Slavery Act 1843 followed.

Wilberforce died on 29 July 1833, three days after the Act passed the Commons.
items.why: Abolition is celebrated as moral progress. The financial mechanics — owners compensated, the enslaved given six more years of forced labour, taxpayers paying off the loan until 2015 — complicate the story without erasing it.
